newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss give Hungary list of wartime account holders.
newsitem.headline: Swiss give Hungary list of wartime account holders.

text.p: Switzerland handed Hungary on Monday the names of 33 people, most of them Holocaust victims, whose bank accounts were declared ownerless after World War Two and credited to Budapest, the foreign ministry in Berne said.

The once-secret list of names and account details, compiled by Federal Archives officials from records kept during a 1960s sweep of Swiss banks for lost Holocaust assets, aims to help the original owners or their heirs get what is rightfully theirs.

"I can confirm that most of the names are connected to Holocaust victims," said a spokesman for the foreign ministry task force coordinating the response to allegations that Swiss banks are hoarding the dormant wealth of people Hitler persecuted.
Officials gave a similar list of 53 people to Poland this month.
A new survey found that half the Swiss would prefer their neutral country's wartime role as a financial centre to remain a chapter of the past left to history books.

Swiss radio's poll of 1,089 people found 46 percent of people surveyed thought national authorities bore moral guilt for their anti-Jewish wartime refugee policy and business ties with the Nazis, but 51 percent wanted not to dredge up the past.

Six out of 10 believed criticism of Switzerland's wartime record by Jewish groups and other critics was overblown, it said, with 38 percent of these blaming foreign politicians, 35 percent foreign media and 26 percent citing Jewish circles as responsible for the row.

"This apparently defensive stance does not necessarily mean that the Swiss are not ready to confront the events of World War Two, but rather that they do not want the discussion forced on them "from abroad'," DRS radio said in a summary of the survey.

Budapest's ambassador to Berne, Pal Gresznaryk, said it was too early to say who the 33 people on the Hungarian list were. He pledged his cpountry would act quickly to find the rightful owners of the wealth.

"The main thing is that Hungary has given assurances that we will do all we can as quickly as possible to find out if these people or their heirs are around so that this matter can be settled as soon as possible," he told Reuters.
"Hungary is very interested in finding the whole truth here and in settling the matter."
Gresznaryk said that after being given the list in Berne he had "a good feeling because we are coming a step closer to clearing up this whole dark story".
He said Budapest, unlike Poland, would not publish the names because this would violate laws on protecting personal data.

An official Swiss report last month showed Berne paid Warsaw 464,000 Swiss francs and Hungary 325,000 francs from dormant accounts in 1975 under accords that settled Swiss claims for property seized by communist regimes after the war.

Switzerland did not supply the owners' names then under a Cold War policy of hiding the identities of account holders from communist rulers for fear they could be in danger, making it impossible for the real owners to be found.

Berne started reviewing the pacts with Poland and Hungary last year after U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato, head of the Senate Banking Committee, accused it of using unclaimed Jewish accounts to pay off Swiss nationals for assets seized by communists.
The Polish and Hungarian payments came from a pool of 10 million Swiss francs found in the 1960s search for accounts left ownerless by Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution.

The task force spokesman said Monday's handover completed the list of known Polish and Hungarian account holders. These were the only two countries to get money from Switzerland under compensation accords.
